G-un.note: 15 casual un, all core; polite hai 8x, but 3 of those (S5L9, S9L14, S10L17) are hai meaning 'here you go' while handing something over, not 'yes'.

G-uun.note: Only 3 casual uun (S1, S3) and one polite iie as a plain 'no' answer (S10L4). Every other iie pushes back or brushes off thanks, so it is listed under G-iya.

G-iya.note: Casual iya is heard only once in all 13 stories (S3L10, 'nah'). The other entries are polite iie, which a learner hears as iie, not iya. The two iie before kochira koso brush off thanks.

G-arigatou.note: Well balanced: 4 casual and 5 polite, including one past form, gozaimashita (S10L7), for a favour done the day before.

G-gomen.note: 6 casual gomen, 3 of them with honto ni ('really sorry'). The polite-apology sumimasen lines also appear under G-sumimasen. Casual gomen and polite sumimasen never meet as a register pair in one exchange.

G-sumimasen.note: All three senses are heard. Excuse me: S5L1, S6L8, S12L1. Sorry: S5L7, S6L9, S9L15, S12L3, S12L8. Thanks: S10L6, S12L11. The 'thanks' sense is the one a learner is most likely to miss.

G-onegai.note: 6 core uses (2 casual, 4 polite), covering ordering (S5L5), accepting an offer (S6L13, S12L15) and 'please do' (S3L11, S8L15). The 3 others are part of the fixed phrase yoroshiku onegai shimasu.

G-douzo.note: 8 uses covering both senses: handing something over (S2, S5, S10) and inviting someone in, to sit or to eat (S9L2, S9L10, S9L12).

G-kochira-koso.note: Both senses are heard: 'likewise' after an introduction (S6L2, S10L10) and 'no, thank YOU / I'm the one who should be sorry' (S10L7, S12L12).

G-ohayou.note: S9L7 talks about the word instead of greeting with it ('it's not morning'), which neatly teaches its time limit. Casual and polite forms are heard back to back in S10L1-4.

G-konnichiwa.note: Heard only 3 times, all in S9-S10. In both stories ohayou is also heard, which gives a time-of-day contrast.

G-jaa-ne.note: 8 casual and 3 polite. The polite form is always the full 'kore de shitsurei shimasu'. A plain 'jaa' (well then) is a different item (E-jaa) and is not counted here.

G-hajimemashite.note: 3 uses, each followed by a name and yoroshiku. Heard in a polite setting (S6) and a casual one (S10).

G-yoroshiku.note: Polite and casual forms both heard. S6L11 shows its second sense, 'thanks ahead' when leaving work, not only on first meeting.

G-moshimoshi.note: Heard as a voicemail opener (S4L1) and as a live two-way phone exchange (S10L13-14).

G-itadakimasu.note: S9L13 uses itadakimasu as a humble verb ('I'll have a bit more'), not as the before-meal phrase. A learner may not notice the difference.

G-gochisousama.note: Polite deshita form once (S9L15), casual twice. S10L2 is said when leaving breakfast, with no itadakimasu before it.

G-oyasumi.note: Used as an actual goodnight only once, as a casual/polite pair at the end of S10. S7L6 quotes it to mean 'straight to bed'.

G-otsukare.note: S10L8 uses otsukare as a hello between colleagues; the English line renders it as 'Hey, Mai!', so the 'good work' sense is hidden there. S11L13 shows the non-work 'you must be worn out' use.

G-hisashiburi.note: The polite form (S9L1) is answered at once by the casual form (S9L2), a good register pair.

G-ki-o-tsukete.romaji: ki o tsukete / ki o tsukete kudasai
G-ki-o-tsukete.note: The polite form 'ki o tsukete kudasai' is never heard. Even the polite neighbour Satou-san (S10L7) uses the plain form.

J-kore.note: 5 core uses (handing over or pointing at a thing in hand); 3 more are the set phrase 'kore de shitsurei shimasu', where kore means 'with this' (I'll leave now), not a thing.

occurrences.form: sore, umi yori motto ii ne

J-sore.note: Both meanings are heard: the thing near the listener (S2L8, S3L2, S5L1) and 'what you said' (S8L11, S12L14). 'sore sore!' means 'exactly!'. 'sorede' is the separate E3 item and only sounds like sore.

occurrences.form: are wa watashi no ja nai yo

J-are.note: Both meanings are heard: something physically over there (S3L7-8, S5L5) and something both speakers know but can't see (the cake in S13L12-13).

J-dore.note: All 4 are core, and each is answered right away with a kore/are/asoko word, which models the question-and-answer pattern.

J-kono.note: 4 core uses. 'kono mae' (S8L12) is a fixed phrase meaning 'last time', not 'this + noun', and a learner could misparse it.

occurrences.form: sono hanashi na n da kedo

J-sono.note: Both meanings are heard: the thing near the listener (S3L6, S5L5) and 'the one mentioned' (S11L13, S13L4). 'sono hanashi' is close to a set phrase.

J-ano.note: Only 3 uses, and 2 of them are the same 'ano kaban'. S1L7 is the shared-knowledge sense; the 'um...' filler 'ano' never occurs.

J-dono.note: 3 core uses, but S11L8 just echoes S11L7, so in practice it is heard in only 2 places.

occurrences.form: koko mo sukoshi samui yo ne

J-koko.note: The best-covered item in J3, with 8 core uses. The 'this point' (in a discussion) sense is never heard; every use is a physical place.

occurrences.form: dochira ni sunderu n desu ka?

J-doko.note: The polite 'dochira' is heard once (S6L3), but S6Q2 asks with 'doko', so the learner has to link the two forms themselves. The 'which part' sense is never heard.

J-soko.note: The weakest item in J3. Only S9L10 is the clear 'there, near you' sense. S11L9 means 'the place you were', and S11L8 points back to the hot spring the speaker herself just named.

occurrences.form: asoko no tsukue ni arimasu yo

J-asoko.note: 5 core uses. S6L9 puts it in the same sentence as koko, which is the cleanest contrast in J3.

J-nani.note: Only 3 story lines ask 'what' (and the 'nan' form appears once, S5L1). The other 3 are 'nani mo' (nothing) and 'nanika' (something), which a learner may mistake for 'what'. Nearly every question uses nani or nan, so the questions do more to train it than the stories.

J-dare.note: 6 core uses, 4 of them in the 'dare no' (whose) pattern. The polite 'donata' is never heard.

J-itsu.note: 4 core uses, all casual 'itsu + verb?' questions. No polite use in the stories.

J-nande.note: 3 of the 4 casual core uses are a bare 'nande?' reaction. The polite 'doushite' appears once in the stories (S12L6) but in 4 questions. S13L8 'nande tte' quotes the question back ('what do you mean, why').

J-ikura.note: 4 core uses, but only S5L3 gets a price answer (yonhyaku en). The other 3 go unanswered ('kke', 'takakunakatta'), so the price reply is heard only once.

occurrences.form: ii desu ne (desu after adjective = politeness only)

F-da.note: 13 core casual da + 22 core polite desu; casual da is never heard bare at sentence end (always + yo/ne/kedo/kara/shi), and casual speakers mostly drop it (kaisha. / koohii. / souji.). n da / n desu / wake da (excluded here, counted under F2) and ja nai forms (I1) are not listed.

F-ka.note: Every core ka is polite (S5, S6, S10, S12); casual ka is never heard marking a question (casual questions use rising intonation or no?), only as musing 'densha ka.' which a learner may mistake for a question. n desu ka x5 and 'desu ka ne' are counted under F2/F3, not here.

occurrences.form: ashita iku ne. (soft declaration of own plan)

F-ne.note: 17 core uses, but 20 of the 37 audible ne are softeners on the speaker's own plans/requests or inside fixed jaa ne / gomen ne / yoroshiku ne, so the agreement-seeking ne is under half of what is heard. The 7 yo ne are excluded.

F-yo.note: 47 stand-alone yo, all asserting something to the listener: news, corrections ('ja nai yo'), reassurance ('ii yo', 'daijoubu da yo') and announced plans ('kau yo'). It is heard in every story except S4 (the voicemail). The 7 yo ne are excluded.

F-yo-ne.note: 7 uses, all core (checking a fact both speakers should know). The only polite one is '-mashita yo ne' (S12L4); 'desu yo ne' is never heard.

occurrences.form: minna ga uchi ni kuru n da
keeki ga mada nai n da
dakara osoku natta n da (listener's realization)
uchi de taberu n da (realization 'oh, so you're...')
ame ni naru n da tte (hearsay frame)

F-n-da.note: 16 core explaining uses, casual and polite. 5 more are the 'oh, so...' realization or hearsay 'n da tte' readings, which look the same but do a different job. n da kedo and n desu ka are counted under their own items.

occurrences.form: dochira ni sunderu n desu ka?

F-no-question.note: 20 uses, all core, but 7 are the set phrase 'ii no? / ii n desu ka?' ('are you sure?'). Possessive 'dare no?' (S3L1), 'sora no?' (S3L3), 'kenta no?' (S3L8, S13L9) sound the same and are not this item, which is a real confusion risk.

F-n-da-kedo.romaji: n da kedo / n desu kedo

occurrences.form: pen ga nai n desu kedo
sono hanashi na n da kedo...
uchi deta n da kedo (narrative background + 'but')

F-n-da-kedo.note: 4 core lead-ins, 2 casual and 2 polite, with 3 of them in the 'na n da kedo' topic shape. Near-misses that are not the item: 'kenta da kedo' (S4L1) and 'daijoubu da kedo' (S8L4).

occurrences.form: dakara, kenji wa mada asa na wake da
dakara watashi ni wa konakatta wake desu ne
sorede, kopii shichatta wake desu ne

F-wake-da.note: 4 uses, all core, and every one follows dakara/sorede, so the learner may treat 'dakara ... wake da' as one fixed frame. The polite pair in S12 come back to back.

F-naa.note: 4 uses, all casual, 2 of them 'ii naa'. The polite 'desu nee' is never heard. No question tests it.

F-kana.romaji: kana / desu ka ne / deshou ka
F-kana.note: 4 casual and 1 polite ('desu ka ne', S12L6). 'deshou ka' is never heard. 'kanari' (S7L7, S10L14, S11L4, S11L6, S13L2) begins with the same sounds and could be misheard.

F-kke.note: 5 uses, all core. 4 attach to a past copula (datta/deshita kke), 2 are the same 'ikura datta kke', and only one attaches to a verb (motteta kke). '-mashita kke' is never heard.

F-tte-kanji.note: 3 uses, all core (past, plain, and question), all casual. 'tte kanji desu' is never heard. Other 'tte' (n da tte S8L8, minna tte S13L5, nande tte S13L8) could blur it. No question tests it.

D-ii.note: 25 uses, 22 core. The irregular past 'yokatta' (4, all in S11) is never tied back to 'ii' on the page. The 'no thanks' use is heard once (S5L7), just after 'ii desu ne' = 'nice' in S5L3, and S5Q3 tests it.

D-daijoubu.note: 8 uses, all core: reassurance, being free on a day ('ashita wa daijoubu'), and asking once ('ashita, daijoubu?'). The very common polite refusal 'daijoubu desu' ('no thanks') is never heard in a story; it appears only in a model answer (S9Q5).

D-dame.note: Only 4 uses, and 2 are the same 'dame ni natchatta' (plans fell through). The 'not allowed' meaning is heard once (S12L14). Casual 'dame da (yo)' is never heard in a story, only in model answers.

D-warui.note: 5 uses, 4 of them in S12. Only the 'at fault' meaning appears; 'bad' (quality) and casual 'warui' as an apology are never heard. Plain 'warui' appears only inside 'warui n desu'; the other 3 are warukunai x2 and warukatta x1.

A-ima.note: 7 uses, all meaning 'now'. Three are 'ima kara' (from now), and it sits next to mada (S4L3 'ima mo mada') and mou (S7L9 'ima wa mou').

A-kyou.note: 23 uses, the most heard item in A1. Two sit inside the fixed sign-off 'kyou wa kore de shitsurei shimasu', where they still mean 'today'.

occurrences.form: kyou wa kore de shitsurei shimasu
kyou wa kore de shitsurei shimasu

A-ashita.note: 13 uses, all core. It is almost always set against kyou in the same stretch (S1, S6L11, S8, S10), so the contrast is well trained.

A-kinou.note: 10 uses, all core. Three are 'kinou no' (yesterday's one) in S12, and kinou is set against kyou in S7L7 and S11L8-L12.

A-mou.note: 10 core 'already' uses, but only one 'not anymore' (S1L6 'mou nai'). The same stories also use mou to mean 'more' (S9L12-13, S11L3-4, S12L13), and nothing flags that difference.

A-mada.note: 10 uses, all core. Both senses are heard: 'still' (7) and 'not yet' (S12L11 'mada kitemasen', S13L10 twice). The standalone polite 'mada desu' is never heard.

A-zutto.note: 4 uses, all core, and three are with a past or negative verb ('zutto konakatta' twice). It is paired with mou in S2L6.

A-yatto.note: Only 3 uses, all core, in just two stories. S7L5 sets it against mou ('yatto ... kaetta kedo, mou yoru datta').

B-chotto.note: 8 uses on its own, 6 meaning 'a bit'. The others are the refusal 'kyou wa chotto...' and the fixed 'chotto ii?'. The mou chotto lines are counted under that item instead.

B-sukoshi.note: Thin. Only 2 plain uses, both in Story 11 (S11L3, S11L16). The third is inside 'mou sukoshi' (a little more) in S9L12.

B-motto.note: 4 uses in 3 lines across two stories. Two are 'motto ii' (even better) and two are the emphatic 'motto da yo, motto!'.

B-mou-chotto.note: 3 core uses: asking for more food, and 'a little colder'. In S12L13 'kaigi made mou chotto' means 'not long now', a different sense.

occurrences.form: kaigi made mou chotto desu kedo

B-sugoku.note: 3 uses, all core, but two are the same phrase 'sugoku yokatta' in S11. The only other one is S9L11 'sugoku oishii desu'.

B-honto-ni.note: 11 uses, but only 6 work as an intensifier, and 4 of those are the apology phrase 'honto ni gomen' / 'hontou ni sumimasen'. Five are the reaction 'honto ni?' or 'hontou desu ka?' (Really?).

B-kekkou.note: 4 uses, all core, always meaning 'quite' and never 'no thanks'. Twice it is 'kekkou kawatta'.

B-kanari.note: 5 uses, all core, in four stories, with adjectives, verbs and amounts. It is heard next to kekkou (S11L6) and mou (S13L2).

B-metcha.note: 3 uses, all core, and two are 'metcha samui/samukatta' in S11. The polite 'totemo' is never heard.

E-demo.note: 12 core, all sentence-initial 'but', heard in 8 stories. The file has 13 stories, not 9, and all 13 were audited. 'X demo' meaning 'even/or something' is never heard.

E-kedo.note: 7 contrastive uses. 5 more are n da kedo / da kedo lead-ins, which overlap the F2 item. Polite contrastive kedo is heard only twice (arimasen kedo S6L9, desu kedo S12L13).

E-noni.note: Only 3 uses, and 2 are the same phrase 'yoyaku shitoita noni' (S11L10 and its echo in S11L11). Both stories have an intent question on it.

E-kara.note: 9 'because' uses spread over 8 stories, 5 of them sentence-final (kara / kara ne). 5 more are kara = 'from' (ima kara x3, kyou kara, asoko kara), which a learner can mishear as 'because'.

E-node.note: Only 3 uses, all in polite speech, 2 of them in Story 12. Casual node is never heard.

E-dakara.note: 5 core uses, 3 of them inside 'dakara ... wake da/desu', so dakara usually rides with F2 wake da. Polite nanode is never heard, and S12L7 uses dakara in polite speech.

E-datte.note: 3 excuse uses, all sentence-initial; S2L3 and S13L15 pair it with a trailing reason (kara, shi). The hearsay 'n da tte' in S8L8 sounds identical but is a different construction.

E-shi.note: 5 trailing reason/add-on uses, all casual, including back-to-back in S3L4-L5. Polite desu shi / -masu shi is never heard.

E-te-and.note: 6 core: sequence (motte deta, yatte, dete, katte) and reason (haitchatte, atte). Half are in S13L14-15. The other te-forms are requests, fixed phrases or te+kuru compounds; te-miru, teru, chau and toku forms are counted under I2.

E-de-sorede.note: 5 sentence-initial casual 'de,' plus 1 polite sorede (S12L8). The particle de (minna de, uchi de, kore de, jibun de: about 8 times) sounds the same and is not counted.

E-jaa.note: 23 'well then / so' uses in 12 of 13 stories (Story 4 has only 'jaa ne'), plus 8 inside the farewell 'jaa ne' (G3 item). This item is saturated.

E-ato.note: 4 'oh, and' uses in 3 stories, all sentence-initial 'ato,' and all spoken by Kenta. 'ato' meaning 'after/later' is never heard, so there is no ambiguity.

I-ta-past.note: Plain -ta is abundant in every story with past events. Polite -mashita is meaningful only in Story 12 (6 forms), apart from the fixed 'arigatou gozaimashita'. Negative pasts (-nakatta, -masen deshita) are marked secondary.

I-nai-negative.note: Plain non-past verb negatives are heard only in Story 13 (shinai x2, hairanai). Most other negatives are past -nakatta, invitations (ikanai, konai, kaerimasen ka) or the fixed sumimasen (11 times). Core polite -masen: arimasen, mottemasen, kitemasen, kimasen deshita.

I-katta-datta.note: Adjective -katta is heard only in Story 11 (yokatta x4, samukatta x3) plus warukatta (S12L14). Noun datta appears in S7, S11 and S13; polite deshita in S9L3, S12L3 and S12L4. Polite '-katta desu' is never heard.

I-kunai-ja-nai.note: Noun 'ja nai' is well heard (10 uses including past and te forms). Adjective -kunai has only one plain non-past adjective (warukunai, S2L4 and polite S12L9); the rest are past (samukunakatta, takakunakatta x2). 'ja nai' as a tag ('isn't it?') is never heard.

I-kute-de.note: Thin: 3 core uses (ame de, samukute, nakute) plus ja nakute in the 'not A but B' sense. Two of the core uses are in Story 11. Na-adjective + de and adjective -kute meaning plain 'and' are barely present.

I-teru.note: 18 uses, both ongoing action (yatteru, shiteru, matteta) and state (motteru, sunderu). Dominated by motte- forms (7) and sunde- forms (3). Polite -temasu/-temasen appears 4 times.

I-te-miru.note: 5 core uses: casual miru x2, the request mite x1, polite mimasu x2. Only S11L16 (itte mite) is tested, through a respond question.

I-chau.note: 7 uses, 6 of them past. 'natchatta' alone is 3 of the 7, and 'dame ni natchatta' is repeated verbatim (S4L2, S10L14). The 'regret/accident' sense dominates; the 'just go ahead and do it all' sense is heard only in S13L16 yatchau.

I-toku.note: 6 core uses: in-advance (tsukuttoku, shitoku, shitoita x2), take-care-of-it (kiitoku) and leave-in-state (mottoku). Polite -tokimasu is never heard in a story line, only in question S8Q3.

occurrences.form: arimashita (nanika arimashita ka = did something happen)

H-aru.note: Well covered (18) in both 'there is' and 'have' senses; 4 are bare negative nai/nakute, which a learner may not map to aru, and the stories also have about 10 copula 'ja nai/ja nakute' that are not aru.

H-iru-exist.note: Thin: only 4 uses, all people being somewhere. The 'have (people, pets)' sense and the negative inai are never heard. The -teru auxiliary is everywhere but is not this item.

H-motsu.note: Strong (10), but every form is -te/-teru (motteru, mottemasu, mottenakatta). The dictionary form motsu and polite mochimasu are never heard. Note that 'motto' (more) in S8L11/S11L4/S11L15 is a different word.

H-sumu.note: Heard only in S6, three times close together, always as the natural -teru form. The sumu/sumimasu forms never occur, and 'sumimasen' (heard about 10 times) sounds similar.

H-suru.note: Strong (15 core), almost all as noun+suru (shigoto, kopii, meeru, yoyaku, souji, kaimono). The bare dictionary form suru is never heard. 11 more are frozen onegai/shitsurei shimasu.

H-yaru.note: Good (8 core), concentrated in S13. 'yatto' (finally) in S7L5/S11L12/S11L13 sounds similar but is a different word. Polite yarimasu is never heard in a story.

H-dekiru.note: Thin: 2 'can do' uses plus 1 'be ready' (a listed sense). There is no negative dekinai and no polite dekimasu.

occurrences.form: narimasu (yonhyaku en ni narimasu, shop formula)

H-naru.note: Adequate (6 core), but formulaic: osoku natta, dame ni natchatta, ame ni naru. Only once does it go with an -ku adjective (osoku).

H-kawaru.note: Heard only as past kawatta (4). S4Q1 and S7Q1 ask 'nani ga kawarimashita ka', but neither S4 nor S7 contains kawaru.

H-iku.note: Good (9), but the past itta never occurs, and polite ikimasu is heard only in questions (S1Q2, S4Q5, S8Q5). 'ikura' (S5L3 etc.) sounds similar.

H-kuru.note: Very strong (19 core) across plain, past, negative and polite forms. The irregular ko-/ki- stems (konai, konakatta, kita) are all heard.

H-kaeru-return.note: Adequate (6), always about going home. It is contrasted with modoru in S7.

H-modoru.note: Adequate (5): 4 are past modotta, 3 of them in S11. The polite form appears only in S7Q2.

H-deru.note: Good (7) for 'leave' (people and trains). The 'appear' sense and polite demasu never occur. The translations render the train deta as 'ran', which hides the leave meaning.

H-hairu.note: Good (6 core), covering enter, bathe in an onsen and fit in. The 'join' sense never occurs.

J-watashi.note: Strong (14). But all three casual uses in S3 come from Sora, who says boku in S13 and is called sora-kun in S9, so the S3 'watashi vs boku' split by speaker is unreliable.

J-san.note: Good (12), mostly in the polite stories S6 and S12, and every question attaches -san to the characters. The competing -kun appears in S9L2 and S9L10 (sora-kun) with no explanation.

J-minna.note: Strong (14: 11 minna, 3 minasan). Two of the minasan come in the near-fixed 'minasan, otsukaresama desu' farewell (S6L11, S10L11).

J-jibun.note: Only 4, but well chosen: jibun no / jibun ni / jibun de, each with a real 'own / myself' contrast. Two of them are question answers (S12Q2/Q3, S13Q2).

J-boku.note: Strong (12), used by Kenta throughout and by Sora in S13. Sora's switch from watashi (S3) to boku (S13) is a speaker-consistency bug.

J-tachi.note: Thin (4), but covers both 'X and the others' (S3) and 'we' (S13). No other pronoun takes -tachi (no watashi-tachi).

J-uchi.note: Very strong (16) for 'home, someone's place'. The 'our (family / company)' sense, e.g. uchi no kaisha, is never heard.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, very strongly in S3L4-L11: uun (L4), un (L7), uun (L9), iya (L10), un (L11), all three members within 8 lines. Also uun then un in S1 (L4, L9). Polite hai and iie are heard together in S12 (hai L2/L5/L8, iie L9/L12/L14). Polite iie is never placed next to casual iya.
chunks.verdict: un is heard 15 times casually and uun 3 times, with S3 a model contrast. Casual iya is heard only once in all 13 stories (S3L10), and 4 of the 5 polite iie push back or brush off thanks rather than simply say 'no'. Only S3Q5 forces a 'no' answer; the other listed questions are yes/no invitations whose model answers open with un/iie or gomen.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. In S5 the whole set appears in one exchange: sumimasen (L1, L7), onegai shimasu (L5, L9), then arigatou gozaimasu + douzo (L10) and arigatou gozaimasu (L11), with onegai, douzo and arigatou in back-to-back lines. S10L5-L7 puts douzo, sumimasen as 'thanks', then iie kochira koso + arigatou gozaimashita side by side. S12L11-12: sumimasen ('thanks') answered by kochira koso. S6L8-9: arigatou gozaimasu, sumimasen ('excuse me'), sumimasen ('sorry'). Casual gomen and polite sumimasen never meet in one exchange.
chunks.verdict: Strong: every item is heard 4-10 times in its core use, sumimasen in all three senses and kochira koso in both senses. Only S10Q4 asks directly about a G2 item; the other questions only call for G2 phrases in their model answers.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S9L1 konnichiwa, then S9L6 ohayou, then S9L7 'ohayou ja nai yo. mou hiru da yo' is an explicit ohayou vs time-of-day contrast. S10 runs the whole day: ohayou (L1-4), konnichiwa + hajimemashite + yoroshiku (L9-10), polite shitsurei shimasu (L11) right before casual jaa ne (L12), and moshimoshi (L13-14). S6L1-2 pairs hajimemashite with yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
chunks.verdict: Every item is heard in its core use, and S9 and S10 give clear register and time contrasts; konnichiwa, hajimemashite and moshimoshi are heard only 3 times each. Only one question (S10Q5, meeting Sora) tests the chunk.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. Before and after a meal: S10L18 itadakimasu, then S10L20 gochisousama; S9L11/L13 itadakimasu, then S9L15 gochisousama deshita. Casual and polite pairs are adjacent: S9L1-2 (ohisashiburi desu / hisashiburi), S10L11-12 (otsukaresama desu / otsukare), S10L21-22 (oyasumi / oyasumi nasai). The meal phrases, oyasumi and otsukare cluster in S10.
chunks.verdict: All six are heard in their core use 2-5 times, with good before/after and casual/polite pairs, though oyasumi is used as a real goodnight only once (S10L21-22) and 'ki o tsukete kudasai' is never heard. Only S7Q5 (replying to itadakimasu) tests the chunk.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, often. In S3L1-L8, kore, sore, are and dore all come within 8 lines while the speakers sort out who owns what, with asoko and kono mixed in. S5L1-L6 runs sore, dore, kore, are, with the customer and staff on opposite sides of the counter. S2L7-L8 pairs kore (handing it over) with sore (the reply). S13L10-L13 has dore twice, then are twice.
chunks.verdict: Strong. All four items have at least 4 core uses, and 'which one?' is answered with a this/that word in the next line several times (S3, S5, S13). The weak spot is testing: only S5Q2 asks about a J1 word, and S5Q5 only uses sore in its model answer. (The file holds 13 stories, not 9; all 13 were audited.)

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes for kono, sono and ano. Kenta holds the key and says 'kono kagi' (S3L3, S3L11), Sora calls the same key 'sono kagi' (S3L6), and 'ano kaban' follows in S3L7 and S3L9. In S5L5-L6 the customer's 'sono keeki' becomes the staff's 'kono keeki', the same item seen from each side. dono is never next to kono, sono or ano in one exchange: S11L7-8 'dono onsen' is followed by 'sono onsen' only at S11L13, and S9L3 has no partner.
chunks.verdict: Good for kono and sono, with two clean speaker-versus-listener flips. ano is thin (3 uses, 2 of them the same bag) and dono is thin and never contrasted (3 uses, one an echo). No question asks about a J4 word directly. S3Q5 reuses 'kono kasa' in its prompt, and S3Q2 only indirectly depends on S3L6 'sono kagi'.

chunks.contrastHeard: koko and asoko are well contrasted. In S6L9 'koko ni wa arimasen kedo, asoko no tsukue ni arimasu' sets them in one sentence (with koko also in S6L7). S3L2-L8 runs doko, asoko, koko, asoko, and S1L2-L7 runs doko, asoko, asoko. soko is never near asoko or koko: in S9 it is 6 lines after koko (L4 then L10), and in S11 5 lines after (L3 then L8-9).
chunks.verdict: koko, asoko and doko are well trained and tested; S6Q3's answer depends on telling koko from asoko, and S13Q2's on S13L14 'koko yatte'. soko is the gap: only 3 uses, the 'near you' sense once (S9L10), never set against asoko, and no question tests it. The polite 'dochira' is heard once (S6L3).

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S13 covers almost the whole set: nani (L1), nande (L3, L7, L8), dare (L5, L8, L9), ikura (L13) and itsu (L14), with dore (L10-11) right after dare (L8-9), the cross-chunk dare/dore pair. The look-alikes nani and nande sit 2 lines apart (S13L1 and S13L3). S11L7-L13 has dono, itsu and ikura, and S8L2-L9 has itsu, nande and doko.
chunks.verdict: All five items have core uses, and S13 contrasts them well. But nani asks 'what' in only 3 story lines (3 more are nani mo or nanika), the polite 'donata' is never heard and 'doushite' only once, and no question tests ikura. The list above leaves out the gist and intent questions that use nani or nan only as a generic frame.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. In S3L6-L7, 'mai no da yo ... kita yo ne' is followed by 'kita ne': yo, yo ne and ne in back-to-back lines. S2L6 has 'matteta yo. chotto ja nai yo ne.' S8L12 has 'daijoubu da yo ... kita yo ne?'. In polite speech, S5L8 has 'daijoubu desu yo. keeki dake desu ne.' and S5L2-L3 has 'desu ka? ... desu yo ... desu ka. ii desu ne ... desu ka?'. Casual ka is never heard as a question, so it is never contrasted with no?.
chunks.verdict: Trained well: yo (47), core ne (17), yo ne (7) and da/desu (35 core) are dense and contrasted line to line, and yo, desu ne and yo ne each get an intent question. The weak spots are that question ka is only polite, more than half of the ne heard are softeners or set phrases (jaa ne, gomen ne), and bare casual 'X da.' is never heard. (The file has 13 stories, not 9; all 13 were audited.)

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S13 has all four close together: L1 'shiteru no?', L4 'na n da kedo... kuru n da', L7 'kuru no?', L9 'wake da', L10 'nai n da'. S12 has the polite set (L1 n desu kedo, L3/L5/L8 n desu, L7-L8 wake desu ne, L15 n desu ka). In S9L8-L9 'yatteta n da yo' leads straight into 'asa na wake da', the explanation and then its conclusion.
chunks.verdict: Trained well: n da (16 core) and no? (20) are frequent in both registers, and n da kedo (4) and wake da (4) are each tested twice. The risks are that 7 of the 20 no? are 'ii no?/ii n desu ka?', possessive 'dare no?/kenta no?' sound the same, and every wake da follows dakara/sorede.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S11 has all four within 11 lines: L5 'ii naa', L8 'dono onsen kana ... ii tte kanji', L14 'ikura datta kke', L15 'yokatta tte kanji?'. S3 has kana (L5), kke (L9) and naa (L10) within 6 lines. S13 has kke (L9), naa (L12) and kke (L13).
chunks.verdict: All four are heard in their core use (naa 4, kana 5, kke 5, tte kanji 3), and S11 and S3 put them side by side. Practice is thin: only kke has a question, naa/kana/tte kanji are never tested, and the polite forms (desu nee, deshou ka, tte kanji desu) are absent.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S2L2-L4 has 'ii yo, ii yo. daijoubu.' then 'warukunai yo'. S10L14 has 'dame ni natchatta. ashita, daijoubu?' in one line. S12L9-L15 has 'warukunai desu yo', then 'sore wa dame desu yo. ... warukatta', then 'ii n desu ka?'. S5 has 'ii' = nice (L3) against 'ii' = no thanks (L7).
chunks.verdict: ii (22 core) and daijoubu (8) are trained well, and all four are contrasted. dame (4, two of them 'dame ni natchatta') and warui (5, four in S12, 'at fault' only) are thin, and the polite refusal 'daijoubu desu' ('no thanks') is never heard. More dame/warui spread across other stories would help, but this alone is no reason to rewrite.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, as pairs. kyou/ashita in S1L7-L9 ('kyou wa yasumi ... ashita wa yatteru'), S6L11, S8L3-L5 and S10L14. kinou/kyou in S7L7 ('kyou wa, kinou yori') and S11L8-L12. ima with kyou in S1L7, with ashita and mada in S4L3, and with mou and kyou in S7L9. No single story has all four words.
chunks.verdict: Strong. All four words are heard often and almost always in their core sense (ima 7, kyou 23, ashita 13, kinou 10), with repeated today/tomorrow and yesterday/today contrasts and many questions that depend on them. No rewrite needed.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S9L7 'mou hiru da yo' and S9L9 'mada asa na wake da' are two lines apart: the clearest mou/mada pair. S7L5 puts yatto and mou together, S2L6 has 'mou zutto', and S4L3 has 'ima mo mada'. But S9L12 'mada aru kara, mou sukoshi' puts mada next to the 'more' sense of mou, which could confuse a learner.
chunks.verdict: Good overall: mou has 10 core uses, mada 10 (both 'still' and 'not yet'), zutto 4, yatto 3. Weak spots: 'not anymore' mou is heard only once, and no question asks the learner to tell mou from mada. Only S2Q3 and S7Q3 really depend on these words.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, and very clearly in S11L3-L4: 'sukoshi samui ... mou chotto samukatta dake?' then 'mou chotto ja nai yo! motto da yo, motto!'. S9L12-L13 pairs 'mou sukoshi' (mother, polite) with 'mou chotto dake' (Sora). S9L4-L5 sets chotto against kekkou, and S2L6 sets chotto against zutto. Plain chotto and plain sukoshi never appear near each other.
chunks.verdict: Adequate, but most of it rests on Story 11. chotto (6 core) and mou chotto (3 core) are fine. motto has only 4 uses in two stories, and sukoshi has just 2 core uses, both in S11. sukoshi needs more uses in other stories.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. Story 11 has all five in one conversation: 'sugoku yokatta ... metcha samukatta' (L2), kanari (L4, L6), 'kekkou atta yo. kanari haitta.' (L6), honto ni (L13), sugoku (L15), metcha (L16). Elsewhere, S13L1-L2 has kekkou then kanari, and S9L5 sets kekkou against chotto.
chunks.verdict: Well trained in Story 11: sugoku, kekkou, kanari and metcha are all used in their core sense. Gaps: sugoku and metcha appear only once each outside S11, the polite 'totemo' is never heard, and honto ni works as an intensifier only 6 times out of 11, 4 of them in the apology phrase 'honto ni gomen'.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, twice. S7L2-L8 has kedo (L2, L4, L5), then demo (L7), then noni (L8). S11L10-L16 has noni (L10, L11), demo (L14, L16) and kedo (L15). Polite contrast: S6L9 arimasen kedo and S12L5 demo / S12L13 desu kedo.
chunks.verdict: Strong for demo (12) and kedo (7 contrastive). noni is adequate (3 uses, 2 intent questions) but repeats one phrase. 5 of 12 kedo are n da kedo lead-ins: S4Q4 and S6Q4 test that F2 use, not kedo = 'but'.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S9L8-L15: datte (L8), dakara (L9), kara (L12), node (L15), with casual kara and polite node 3 lines apart. S2L3-L4: datte...kara, then dakara. S7L3-L6: kara, shi, dakara. S13L13-L15: shi, then datte...shi. Casual kara and polite node are never contrasted within one speaker's register.
chunks.verdict: kara is well trained (9 'because' uses, but 5 'from' homophones). dakara, datte and shi are adequate (3-5 each); node is thin (3, polite only). Only datte has an intent question; shi, node and dakara are never targeted (dakara only sits inside the wake-da questions S9Q4/S12Q4). Polite nanode and desu shi are never heard.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S11L13 has jaa and de in one line. S13L10-L16 has de + ato (L10), jaa (L11, L12, L14, L16) and the te-chain yatte/dete/katte (L14-L15). S8L13-L16 has de, ato, jaa ne. S7L4 has de + motte deta.
chunks.verdict: jaa is saturated (23 core). de/sorede (6) and ato (4) are adequate, with ato tested once. te as 'and then' rests mostly on S13L14-L15 plus 2 reason uses (haitchatte, atte). No question targets de.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes, concentrated. S12L3 has 'ja nakatta desu. kinou no deshita.' side by side. S11L1 has yokatta / samukunakatta; S11L14-L15 has takakunakatta / samukatta / yokatta; S11L4 has samukute + ja nai. Present vs past negative: S13 shinai vs S7/S12 konakatta. Story 11 is the hub for katta/kunai/kute.
chunks.verdict: -ta and ja nai are well trained. Plain non-past verb -nai is core only in Story 13 (3 uses) and is otherwise mostly past or invitation forms. Adjective -katta/-kunai lean almost entirely on Story 11, and kute/de is thin (3 core). No intent question targets any I1 form; only detail questions hinge on them.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. S3L9-L11 contrasts the same verb: motteta / mottenakatta / kiitoku / mottoku (teru vs toku). S4L2-L5 has natchatta, haitchatte, shiteru, tsukuttoku in 4 lines. S12L6-L13 has shichaimashita, shichatta, shite mimasu, kitemasen, yatte mimasu. S13L13-L16 has itte miru and yatchau.
chunks.verdict: Well trained overall: teru 18, chau 7, toku 6, te-miru 5, with good same-verb contrasts. Weak spots: chau is 6/7 past and its non-regret sense is heard once; polite -tokimasu is never heard; no question probes chau's nuance (S8Q3 is the only direct form question, on toku).

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. aru vs iru: S6L7 imasu (people) then S6L8–L9 nai / arimasen / arimasu (pens), and S11L5–L6 atta (onsen) then S11L9 ita (person). aru vs motsu for 'have': S3L4 motteru next to S3L5 aru, and S10L3–L5 mottemasu / mottemasen / uchi ni mada arimasu. sumu vs iru: S6L3–L7 sunderu ×3, then imasu.
chunks.verdict: aru (18) and motsu (10) are well trained, with good have/there-is contrasts. iru is thin (4, never 'have people/pets', and no question tests it), and sumu lives entirely in S6. motsu is never heard as motsu/mochimasu.

chunks.contrastHeard: suru vs yaru for the same activity sit side by side: S13L1 'nani shiteru no' / S13L2 'mou kanari yatta', S13L9–L16 (souji shiteru, dore yaru, yatte, shinai, yatchau), and S12L13 'dare ga shimasu ka … yatte mimasu' in one line. naru and dekiru are 2 lines apart in S8L8/S8L10. naru vs kawaru (become vs change) are never near each other.
chunks.verdict: suru (15 core, plus 11 frozen onegai/shitsurei shimasu) and yaru (8 core), with a good S13 contrast, are strong. naru is adequate but formulaic. dekiru (3) and kawaru (4, past kawatta only, untested; S4Q1/S7Q1 ask about kawaru in stories that lack it) are thin.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. kaeru vs modoru: S7L3 'uchi ni modotta' and S7L5 'uchi ni kaetta', 2 lines apart. iku/kuru: S1L2–L10 (iku, kita, kaeru, iku) and S8L1–L14 (ikanai, iku ×3, kuru, kita, kuru). deru / modoru / hairu in one line at S13L15 ('dete … modoru … hairanai'). deru and modoru recur together in S11L10–L13.
chunks.verdict: Well trained overall. kuru (19 core) is excellent, and kaeru, modoru, deru and hairu get 5–7 uses each with real contrasts. Gaps: iku never in the past (itta) or polite (ikimasu) in a story line; deru 'appear' and hairu 'join' absent; deru tested only via the S11 gist.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. watashi vs jibun in the same line: S3L4 'watashi no ja nai yo. jibun no kagi, motteru shi' and S12L14 'watashi ga warukatta node, kopii wa jibun de shimasu'; also S12L6–L7 jibun ni / watashi ni wa. minna vs minasan contrast only across stories (casual S3/S8/S13 vs polite S6/S10/S12). -san vs bare name sit adjacent: S3L6 'mai-tachi' / S3L9 'mai-san-tachi'.
chunks.verdict: Strong for watashi (14), -san (12) and minna (14), and jibun (4) is few but sharply contrasted with watashi. Weak points: Sora's casual watashi in S3 contradicts his boku in S13, and the unexplained -kun in S9.

chunks.contrastHeard: Yes. boku vs watashi in one exchange: S3 has Kenta saying boku (L5, L9, L11) against Sora saying watashi (L2, L4, L8), but S13 has Sora saying boku, so the contrast is muddied. boku-tachi / minna / uchi are packed into S13L3–L5 ('boku-tachi … minna ga uchi ni kuru … boku-tachi no uchi ni? minna tte, dare?').
chunks.verdict: boku (12) and uchi (16) are strongly trained, though uchi only means 'home' and its 'our (family / company)' sense never appears. -tachi is thin (4) but well placed. Fix Sora's watashi in S3, or make Sora consistently one gender, so the watashi/boku speaker contrast holds.
